# Lab 3: Repeat Annotation and Scaffolding

## Repeat Annotation

Let’s look at the repeat profile of our genome, and soft mask the repeats to lowercase since many downstream steps will require this.

| mkdir Heliconius\_doris/repeat\_results |
| :---- |

Let’s install our programs:

| conda install \-c bioconda repeatmasker repeatmodeler |
| :---- |

**DO NOT RUN REPEATMODELER AND REPEATMASKER. COPY THE FINAL FILES FROM MY FOLDERS TO ANSWER THE QUESTIONS.** 

We will use RepeatModeller to model the repeats based on our genome. RepeatModeler is a de novo transposable element (TE) family identification and modeling package. At the heart of RepeatModeler are three de-novo repeat finding programs ( RECON, RepeatScout and LtrHarvest/Ltr\_retriever ) which employ complementary computational methods for identifying repeat element boundaries and family relationships from sequence data.

| BuildDatabase \-name H\_doris Heliconius\_doris.bp.p\_ctg.fa RepeatModeler \\ \-dir repeat\_results \\  \-threads \${SLURM\_CPUS\_PER\_TASK} \\  \-database H\_doris \-quick |
| :---- |

**What does BuildDatabase do?** 

This program takes a while to run so let’s just download the relevant fasta file output from my directory. 

| /home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/Comparative\_Genomics\_Course/Heliconius\_doris/repeat\_results/consensi.fa.classified |
| :---- |

   
RepeatMasker is a program that screens DNA sequences for interspersed repeats and low complexity DNA sequences. The output of the program is a detailed annotation of the repeats that are present in the query sequence as well as a modified version of the query sequence in which all the annotated repeats have been masked.

Run a job requesting 24 cores, 5gb, for 5 hours. Change the paths to where these files are on your system.

| RepeatMasker \-qq \-pa 12 \\\-lib consensi.fa.classified \\\-dir H\_doris\_mask2 Heliconius\_doris.bp.p\_ctg.fa \-xsmall |
| :---- |

We are using the RMBlast database to mask repeats, which uses 4 cores per use, therefore if we request 24 cores, we want to run 24/4=6 runs in parallel (pa).   
**What does xsmall do?**

This job will take an hour to run, let’s look at the output files instead. Copy the following file and Look at the results. 

| /home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/Comparative\_Genomics\_Course/Heliconius\_doris/repeat\_results/H\_doris\_mask2/ |
| :---- |

**What percent of the genome is repetitive? What kind of repeats are present and at what proportion?**

## Scaffolding

Genome scaffolding is the process of ordering and orienting contigs (continuous stretches of DNA sequence) into a higher-level structure, like a chromosome. Typically you want to identify chromosome structure with Hi-C data for analysis\! This can be pricey so an alternative option for now, we will scaffold your contigs to a reference genome and explore how syntenic they are to each other.

We see that karyotype data for all of our individuals is consistent, which means we can take a comparative approach to scaffolding with higher accuracy.   
![][image1]  
Table S1. Karyotype is consistent across species.

There is a well established reference genome for H. sara that we can compare our genome to. 

On NCBI, find the *Heliconius sara* chromosome-level reference genome assembly. 

Click FTP near the top of the page for an easy way to grab the link address. You will see a list of files. ![][image2]The fasta file has the ending “genomic.fna”.  Copy the link address (right click \- copy link address) and download that to your Comparative genomics directory.

| cd .. wget \[link\] |
| :---- |

This is a compressed file format so we can’t look into it without using special tools. Let’s just uncompress it. 

FASTA format files take the form:  
 \>Name  
Sequence

We can pull out just the sequence names to make sure this is a chromosome level file.

Grep is used to search text for lines matching a specified pattern. Here we will see lines that start with (^)  this symbol \> and print those.

| gunzip \[filename\]\_genomic.fna.gz grep "^\>" \[filename\]\_genomic.fna |
| :---- |

**There are many chromosome scaffolds, which would presumably be the whole genome. However, there are also scaffolds with names like scaffold\_\#\#\# that make up this genome assembly. What could these be?**  
**How many chromosomes does *H. sara* have?**

RagTag is a program that allows us to scaffold a query genome (our H. doris) with a reference (like H. sara). 

Take a look at the GitHub to understand what each of these processes do: [https\://github.com/malonge/RagTag/](https://github.com/malonge/RagTag/) Today, we will be using the scaffold capability- “Scaffolding is the process of ordering and orienting draft assembly (query) sequences into longer sequences. Gaps (stretches of "N" characters) are placed between adjacent query sequences to indicate the presence of unknown sequence…”

If you did not install RagTag in Lab 1, do so now with conda in your genome-assembly package. Let’s see what we can do with it:

| ragtag.py \-h  |
| :---- |

RagTag does not alter input query sequence in any way and only orders and orients sequences, joining them with gaps.

| ragtag.py scaffold \-h  |
| :---- |

Since our reference is divergent, let’s use minimap to align the reference and query. We can see here that we can specify in minimap the level of sequence divergence between our query and reference with the \-x asm option. 

 [https\://lh3.github.io/minimap2/minimap2.html](https://lh3.github.io/minimap2/minimap2.html)

| asm5 | Long assembly to reference mapping (\-k19 \-w19 \-U50,500 \--rmq \-r1k,100k \-g10k \-A1 \-B19 \-O39,81 \-E3,1 \-s200 \-z200 \-N50). Typically, the alignment will not extend to regions with 5% or higher sequence divergence. Use this preset if the average divergence is not much higher than 0.1%. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **asm10** | Long assembly to reference mapping (**\-k19** **\-w19 \-U50,500 \--rmq \-r1k,100k \-g10k \-A1 \-B9 \-O16,41 \-E2,1 \-s200 \-z200** **\-N50**). Use this if the average divergence is around 1%. |
| **asm20** | Long assembly to reference mapping (**\-k19** **\-w10 \-U50,500 \--rmq \-r1k,100k \-g10k \-A1 \-B4 \-O6,26 \-E2,1 \-s200 \-z200** **\-N50**). Use this if the average divergence is around several percent. |

Use asm5 when they are very closely related (e.g., different strains), asm10 for within-species/population, and asm20 for different species

Let’s first rename our reference sequence scaffolds for ease. We’ll do this using a complex sed command, which performs transformations on files line-by-line. I will explain how you might typically use sed shortly but here is the line for now:

| sed '/^\>OU/ s/^\>.\*chromosome: /\>/' GCA\_917862395.2\_iHelSar1.2\_genomic.fna \> HelSar1.2\_genomic.fna |
| :---- |

* **`/^>OU/`**: Only acts on lines that start with "\>OU".  
* **`s/^>.*chromosome: />/`**: Substitutes everything from the start of the line through "chromosome: " with a single `>`.

   
Verify that it did what you want:

| grep "^\>" HelSar1.2\_genomic.fna |
| :---- |

RagTag.sh

| \#\!/bin/bash\#SBATCH \--job-name=ragtag       \# Name of the job\#SBATCH \--nodes=1                        \# Run on a single node\#SBATCH \--cpus-per-task=24             \# Number of threads for the task\#SBATCH \--reservation=ddebaun\_37 \#SBATCH \--mem=5G                        \# Total memory\#SBATCH \--time=00:10:00                  \# Max runtime (HH:MM:SS)\#SBATCH \--mail-type=ALL                  \# When to send email\#SBATCH \--mail-user=\[name\]@amnh.org        \# Email address\#SBATCH \--output=slurm-%x\_%j.out    \# Stdout file (jobname\_jobid.out) \#make sure to activate teh conda environment in the script source \~/.bash\_profile conda activate genome-assembly reference=HelSar1.2\_genomic.fna query=Heliconius\_doris/Heliconius\_doris.bp.p\_ctg.fa ragtag.py scaffold \-t \${SLURM\_CPUS\_PER\_TASK} \-u \$reference \$query \-o Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara \--mm2-params '-x asm20' |
| :---- |
|  |

Open the log file and make sure everything worked out. Don’t take a ‘COMPLETED’ job status to mean that no error occurred. 

Change into the results directory. Make sure the ragtag.scaffold.err file is empty. We can look at the stats file as well to understand how that run went.

**How many Ns were placed to scaffold the sequences?**

## Synteny

Now that we have contigs that are both chromosome-level, we can visualize the synteny between these contigs. 

First, we must do some housekeeping by renaming the contigs from RagTag to have the same name as they do in the reference, so let’s remove the ‘\_RagTag’.

Let’s use the sed command again. At its most basic it looks like this:

| sed 's/\$FIND/\$REPLACEMENT/g' \$file \> \$newfile |
| :---- |

Where FIND is some text you want to find and replace with REPLACEMENT. This can write to a new file with the \> option or to the same file with sed \-i option (be careful though\!). The s is for string and the g is for global, meaning all cases will be replaced, remove this if you just want the first replaced.

Here we replace the FIND string with nothing.

| sed 's/\_RagTag//g' ragtag.scaffold.fasta \> Hdoris\_rename.scaffold.fasta |
| :---- |

Next we will do some fancy work to get just our chromosomes into a FASTA for both the reference and the query. Let’s make a list of the chromosomes that we want to examine synteny of. We will make use of the pipe command to do a few things at once.

| cd .. \# got your Comparative\_Genomics\_Course foldergrep "^\>" HelSar1.2\_genomic.fna \| grep \-v "\>CAK" \| sed 's/\>//' \> chrom\_list.txt |
| :---- |

**`grep "^>"`**: Pulls all the header lines from your FASTA file.  
**`grep -v ">CAK"`**: The `-v` flag stands for "invert-match." It tells the computer to **discard** any line that contains "\>CAK".  
**`sed 's/>//'`**: Removes the `>` symbol from the beginning of the remaining lines so that your list is just clean names.  
**`> chrom_list.txt`**: Saves those names into your text file.

Now, we will extract just these chromosomes from the fasta files. We will load a preavailable program, or module called Samtools to easily extract the sequences we want.

| module load Samtools/samtools-1.11samtools faidx HelSar1.2\_genomic.fna \-r chrom\_list.txt \> HelSar1.2\_chrs.fasamtools faidx Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/Hdoris\_rename.scaffold.fasta \-r chrom\_list.txt \> Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/Hdoris\_rename.chr.fasta |
| :---- |

**What can samtools faidx be used for?**  
**Which flag/option does \-r indicate? Write the line as it is written in the manual/help.**

SyRI expects chromosome names to begin with letters rather than numbers, otherwise it can misinterpret them. Let’s quickly replace \> with \>Chr to solve this. We will use the \-i command to do this in the same file. ***`-i` edits files permanently. Double-check filenames before running.***

| sed \-i 's/\>/\>Chr/g' HelSar1.2\_chrs.fased \-i 's/\>/\>Chr/g' Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/Hdoris\_rename.chr.fasta |
| :---- |

We now have a bunch of files for HelSara in our home directory, let’s give these their own directory to keep tidy.

| mkdir HelSar1mv HelSar1\* GCA\_917862395.2\_iHelSar1.2\_genomic.fna HelSar1  |
| :---- |

Now we are going to make a script where we:

1. Align the chromosome-level genomes to each other using minimap  
2. Use Syri to interpret synteny based on this alignment

Let’s install SyRi [https\://github.com/schneebergerlab/syri](https://github.com/schneebergerlab/syri)

| conda install bioconda::syri bioconda::plotsr |
| :---- |

Notice how we are upgrading and downgrading packages sometimes when we install new programs, this is why we want to be super careful when working with package managers because these up/down grades may render other programs we installed unusable. Typically, you want to make a new conda environment for each program you install unless they require totally independent dependencies. You can always click ‘n’ instead of ‘y’ if you see that you will need to change a dependency and choose to install in a new environment. 

Let’s store our results here:

| mkdir Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/synteny\_results |
| :---- |

Synteny.sh

| \#\!/bin/bash\#SBATCH \--job-name minimap\#SBATCH \--nodes=1\#SBATCH \--cpus-per-task=24\#SBATCH \--mem=40gb \#SBATCH \--reservation=ddebaun\_37\#SBATCH \--time=30:00:00\#SBATCH \--mail-type=ALL\#SBATCH \--mail-user=\[name\]@amnh.org \#SBATCH \--output=slurm-%x\_%j.outsource \~/.bash\_profileexport PATH=/home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/miniconda3/bin:\$PATH \#change to your pathconda activate genome-assemblyREF="HelSar1/HelSar1.2\_chrs.fa"QUERY="Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/Hdoris\_rename.chr.fasta"OUT="Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/synteny\_results/doris\_sara\_chr.sam" \#Align with Minimap2minimap2 \-ax asm20 \--eqx \-t \${SLURM\_CPUS\_PER\_TASK} \$REF \$QUERY \> \$OUT \#Run SyRIsyri \-c \$OUT \-r \$REF \-q \$QUERY \-F S \--prefix doris\_vs\_sara\_ \#make a file of genome pathsecho \-e "\${REF}\\tSara" \> doris\_vs\_sara.genomes \#\> creates a fileecho \-e "\${QUERY}\\tDoris" \>\> doris\_vs\_sara.genomesplotsr \--sr doris\_vs\_sara\_syri.out \--genomes doris\_vs\_sara.genomes |
| :---- |

Now we can view the results of this output. Let’s open a new terminal window on the local computer and scp the pdf file. (Edit the paths appropriately).

| scp ddebaun@mendel-master.sdmz.amnh.org:/home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/Comparative\_Genomics\_Course/plotsr.pdf  \~/Documents/examplefolder/ |
| :---- |

**Are chromosomes mostly collinear? How many large-scale inversions do you see? Duplications?** 

Now check the .summary file. **How many inversions and duplications are there actually?** This will include smaller events.

**What might be going on in the sex chromosome?**

Let’s do some quick cleanup of that last run, putting it in our synteny results directory

| mv doris\_vs\_sara\* plotsr.\* Heliconius\_doris\_ragtagsara/synteny\_results/ |
| :---- |

Congrats you have now assembled a long read whole genome and explored synteny\!\! Tomorrow we will tackle variant calling for short read analysis.
